items.text: What is the shape of a normal distribution curve?
items.explanation: A normal (Gaussian) distribution is characterized by a symmetric, unimodal, bell-shaped probability density curve centered at the mean.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4 (Probability Distributions)

items.text: In a normal distribution, the mean, median, and mode are:
items.explanation: Because the normal distribution is perfectly symmetrical about its center, the mean, median, and mode all coincide at the exact central peak.
items.keyConcept: Equality of mean, median, mode in normal distribution
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: What is the total area under the normal distribution curve?
items.explanation: The total area under any continuous probability density curve, including the Gaussian distribution, represents the sum of all probabilities and is strictly equal to 1.0 (100%).
items.keyConcept: Total probability area under normal curve = 1
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: The mean of the standard normal distribution is:
items.explanation: By definition, the standard normal distribution (Z-distribution) has a mean (μ) of 0 and a standard deviation (σ) of 1.
items.keyConcept: Standard normal distribution parameters: μ = 0, σ = 1
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: In a normal distribution, about 68% of the data falls within:
items.explanation: Under the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule for a normal distribution, approximately 68.27% of observations fall within ±1 standard deviation of the mean (μ ± 1σ).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: In a normal distribution, about 95% of the data falls within:
items.explanation: Under the empirical rule, approximately 95.45% of observations in a normal distribution lie within ±2 standard deviations of the mean (strictly 95% within ±1.96σ).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: What does a z-score of 0 indicate?
items.explanation: A z-score measures how many standard deviations an observation is from the mean (z = (x - μ)/σ). A z-score of 0 indicates that the observed value equals the population mean.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: A positive z-score means the value is:
items.explanation: A positive z-score indicates that the observed measurement lies above (to the right of) the mean, whereas a negative z-score indicates a value below the mean.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: A leptokurtic distribution has:
items.explanation: Kurtosis measures tailedness. A leptokurtic distribution (excess kurtosis > 0) features a sharp, slender central peak and heavy/fat tails with higher probability of extreme values compared to a normal distribution.
items.citation: Altman, Practical Statistics for Medical Research, Ch. 3

items.text: In a right-skewed distribution:
items.explanation: In a right-skewed (positively skewed) distribution, extreme values pull the tail to the right, pulling the mean highest, followed by the median, then the mode (Mean > Median > Mode).
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 2

items.text: In a normal distribution, most of the data lies:
items.explanation: Because the normal distribution peaks at the center, the greatest concentration of data points (density) is clustered symmetrically around the mean.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: The heights of a population of adult women are normally distributed with a mean of 64 inches and a standard deviation of 3 inches. What is the z-score for a woman who is 70 inches tall?
items.explanation: Using the formula z = (x - μ)/σ = (70 - 64)/3 = 6/3 = +2.0, meaning her height is exactly 2 standard deviations above the population mean.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: In a normal distribution with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, what percentage of values fall between 85 and 115?
items.explanation: The interval [85, 115] corresponds to μ ± 1σ (100 ± 15). Under the empirical rule, approximately 68% of the data in a normal distribution falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: The weights of bags of flour are normally distributed with a mean of 5 kg and a standard deviation of 0.5 kg. If a bag weighs 6 kg, what is its z-score?
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 4

items.text: Confidence intervals can be built for means - but not for percentages.
items.explanation: Confidence intervals can be constructed for continuous parameters (means, differences between means) as well as categorical parameters (proportions, percentages, odds ratios).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 6 (Estimation)

items.text: Using the same data, a confidence interval will get wider if the confidence level is increased.
items.explanation: To achieve greater certainty (e.g., increasing confidence from 95% to 99%), the critical multiplier (z* or t*) increases, widening the margin of error and the resulting interval.
items.keyConcept: Relationship between confidence level and interval width
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: A confidence interval indicates the probability that the population parameter lies somewhere between the numerical end points of the CI.
items.explanation: In frequentist statistics, the population parameter is a fixed constant, not a random variable. A specific calculated interval either contains the parameter or does not (probability 0 or 1). The 95% confidence level describes the long-run capture rate of the procedure across repeated samples.
items.citation: Altman, Practical Statistics for Medical Research, Ch. 7

items.text: To interpret a confidence interval correctly, you must imagine that lots of samples are drawn from the population.
items.explanation: Frequentist confidence intervals are grounded in sampling theory: if 100 independent random samples were drawn and a 95% CI computed from each, approximately 95 of those intervals would capture the true parameter.
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: If someone says "52 ± 3," the 3 might be referring to the SD or it might be referring to the SEM.
items.explanation: In medical and scientific literature, the notation 'mean ± X' is frequently used for either standard deviation (SD) or standard error of the mean (SEM), requiring authors to specify which metric is reported.
items.citation: Altman DG. Statistics with confidence. BMJ Books; 2000

items.text: Why do we use inferential statistics?
items.explanation: Inferential statistics uses sample data to make generalized inferences, point and interval estimates, and hypothesis tests about unknown population parameters.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: The sample mean x̄ is called a ________ of the population mean μ.
items.explanation: A point estimate is a single sample statistic (such as x̄) that serves as the best point-value estimate of an unknown population parameter (μ).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: A 95% confidence interval for the mean number of televisions per American household is (1.15, 4.20). Which statement is correct about this confidence interval?
items.explanation: Confidence applies to the estimation method across repeated samples; we state that we are 95% confident that the fixed, unknown population parameter lies within the calculated interval.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: Population A has a mean of 1,000 and a standard deviation of 70, while Population B has a mean of 1,200 and a standard deviation of 62. For samples of size 35, then the standard error of A will be:
items.explanation: Standard error is calculated as SE = σ / √n. With equal sample sizes (n = 35), Population A has a higher standard deviation (σA = 70 > σB = 62), so SEA = 70/√35 ≈ 11.83 is larger than SEB = 62/√35 ≈ 10.48.
items.keyConcept: Standard error comparison with equal sample size
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: Which of the following is most likely to result in a larger standard error if everything else is held constant?
items.explanation: Standard error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size (SE = σ/√n). Therefore, reducing the sample size increases the standard error.
items.keyConcept: Sample size inversely related to standard error
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: A researcher is going to draw a sample of 150 values from a population. The researcher wants to find probabilities for the sample mean. Which of the following statements is true?
items.explanation: By the Central Limit Theorem, if the sample size is sufficiently large (n ≥ 30, and here n = 150), the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal regardless of the underlying population shape.
items.keyConcept: Central Limit Theorem sample size condition
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: You draw a sample and calculate the sample mean. Which of the following is true?
items.explanation: Larger samples reduce sampling variability (SE = σ/√n), clustering sample means tighter around the true population mean and producing greater precision.
items.keyConcept: Precision increases with larger sample size
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: Suppose 10,000 random samples of the same size are drawn from a population having M=50 & SD=4. Each sample's mean is computed and then displayed in a sampling distribution. About what fraction of the sample means would lie within one standard error of 50?
items.explanation: By the empirical rule of the normal distribution, approximately 68.27% of observations fall within ±1 standard error of the mean. The fraction 2/3 ≈ 66.7% is the closest standard fractional approximation to 68%.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 5

items.text: A random sample of 50 students at one school was obtained and each selected student was given an IQ test. These data were used to measure IQ score with a 95% confidence interval between [96.656, 106.422]. How do you interpret this confidence interval?
items.explanation: Correct CI interpretation specifies: (1) the level of confidence (95%), (2) the parameter of interest (true population mean IQ), and (3) the calculated lower and upper bounds [96.66, 106.42].
items.keyConcept: Interpretation of confidence interval for a population mean
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: A sample of university students was surveyed about their seatbelt usage. A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all university students who always wear their seatbelt was computed to be [0.612, 0.668]. How do you interpret this confidence interval?
items.explanation: For proportions, a confidence interval is interpreted as 95% confidence that the true population proportion lies within the specified bounds [61.2%, 66.8%].
items.keyConcept: Interpretation of confidence interval for a population proportion
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 6

items.text: The purpose of hypothesis testing is to:
items.explanation: Hypothesis testing uses sample evidence to evaluate whether an observed effect is statistically significant or could have occurred simply by random chance.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7 (Hypothesis Testing)

items.text: If the null hypothesis is false then which of the following is accepted?
items.explanation: In statistical hypothesis testing, the null (H0) and alternative (H1/Ha) hypotheses are mutually exhaustive; rejecting a false null hypothesis leads to accepting the alternative hypothesis.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The probability of Type I error is referred as:
items.explanation: The probability of committing a Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis) is denoted by alpha (α), which also represents the significance level of the test.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: A Type I error occurs when we:
items.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive error that occurs when a researcher rejects the null hypothesis when it is in fact true.
items.citation: Altman, Practical Statistics for Medical Research, Ch. 8

items.text: A Type II error occurs when we:
items.explanation: A Type II error (β) is a false negative error that occurs when a researcher fails to reject (retains) a null hypothesis that is actually false.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The rejection probability of Null Hypothesis when it is true is called as:
items.explanation: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis is the level of significance (α), typically chosen as 0.05 or 0.01 prior to conducting the test.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: In a two-tail test for the population mean, if the null hypothesis is rejected when the alternative is true then:
items.explanation: When the alternative hypothesis is true and the null hypothesis is rejected, the test has correctly identified a true effect, representing a correct decision (probability = power = 1 - β).
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: If we reject the null hypothesis, we conclude that:
items.explanation: Rejecting the null hypothesis indicates that the sample data provide sufficient statistical evidence at the chosen significance level to support the alternative hypothesis.
items.keyConcept: Conclusion upon rejecting the null hypothesis
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The p-value of a test is the:
items.explanation: By definition, the p-value is the lowest significance level (α) at which the observed sample data would lead to rejection of the null hypothesis.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: Which of the following statements about hypothesis testing is true?
items.explanation: The decision rule states that if p > α, we fail to reject H0; if p ≤ α, we reject H0. (Option B describes Type I error; confidence level is 1 - α; power is 1 - β).
items.keyConcept: Decision rule with p-value and significance level
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: If the p-value is 0.04, and the significance level (α) is 0.05, what should be the conclusion?
items.explanation: Because the p-value (0.04) is less than the significance level (α = 0.05), the result is statistically significant and the researcher rejects the null hypothesis.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The power of a statistical test is defined as:
items.explanation: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, mathematically defined as 1 - β, where β is the probability of committing a Type II error.
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: State the null hypothesis (Ho) and alternative hypothesis (Ha) in terms of the appropriate parameter (μ or π): "Prevalence of Diabetes in Egypt is 20%".
items.explanation: Prevalence is a proportion (categorical parameter denoted π or p). The null hypothesis states that the population proportion equals the specified value (0.20), while the two-tailed alternative states it differs from 0.20.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: State the null hypothesis (Ho) and alternative hypothesis (Ha) in terms of the appropriate parameter (μ or π): "60% of Egyptian females, compared to 30% of males suffer from Anaemia".
items.explanation: Comparing anaemia prevalence between females and males tests two independent population proportions. The null asserts no sex difference (π1 = π2).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: State the null hypothesis (Ho) and alternative hypothesis (Ha) in terms of the appropriate parameter (μ or π): "The safe dose of Drug X is 30 mg/Kg body weight".
items.explanation: Dose is a continuous quantitative variable represented by the population mean (μ). The null hypothesis posits that the true mean is 30 mg/kg.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: State the null hypothesis (Ho) and alternative hypothesis (Ha) in terms of the appropriate parameter (μ or π): "Systolic blood pressure increases with age in adults (>18 years)".
items.explanation: Testing an increasing trend evaluates the association between two continuous variables. The null hypothesis specifies no relationship (ρ = 0), while a directional alternative posits a positive correlation (ρ > 0).
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 11

items.text: The hypothesis that assumes no effect or no difference is called the ___ hypothesis.
items.explanation: The null hypothesis (H0) represents the baseline claim of no treatment effect, no difference between groups, or no association.
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis is known as ___ error.
items.explanation: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error (α), corresponding to a false positive finding.
items.citation: Altman, Practical Statistics for Medical Research, Ch. 8

items.text: If the p-value is less than or equal to 0.05, we ___ the null hypothesis.
items.explanation: When the p-value is at or below the significance threshold (α = 0.05), the observed effect is deemed statistically significant and the decision is to reject H0.
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: The ___ of a test is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.
items.explanation: Statistical power (1 - β) measures the test's ability to detect a true difference and correctly reject H0.
items.citation: Kirkwood & Sterne, Essential Medical Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: If the power of a test is 0.90, then the probability of making a Type II error (β) is ___.
items.explanation: Because Power = 1 - β, the probability of a Type II error is β = 1 - Power = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10 (or 10%).
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: Match each hypothesis testing term with its correct definition:
items.explanation: Null hypothesis (H0) states no difference; alternative (H1) posits an effect; Type I error (α) is a false positive (rejecting true null); Type II error (β) is a false negative (retaining false null).
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: A study tests whether a new drug improves sleep quality compared to a placebo. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference. The analysis produces a p-value of 0.08. Interpret the p-value. Decide what conclusion the researchers should draw at α = 0.05, and identify what type of error could occur.
items.explanation: When p > α, fail to reject H0. The only potential error when retaining H0 is a Type II error (false negative).
items.keyConcept: P-value interpretation and Type II error risk
items.citation: Rosner, Fundamentals of Biostatistics (8th ed.), Ch. 7

items.text: A medical researcher performs a hypothesis test comparing the mean recovery time for two surgical techniques. The null hypothesis claims both have the same recovery time. The data result in a test statistic with a p-value of 0.03. What is the appropriate decision at α = 0.05, and what type of error could still occur?
items.explanation: When p ≤ α, reject H0. The only potential error when rejecting H0 is a Type I error (false positive).
items.keyConcept: P-value significance and Type I error risk
items.citation: Daniel & Cross, Biostatistics (11th ed.), Ch. 7
